unverified_facts: Livyatan melvillei was formally described in 2010 by Olivier Lambert and colleagues in Nature.
The holotype skull was found in 2008 at Cerro Colorado, Pisco Formation, southern Peru.
The fossil is about 9.9-8.9 million years old (late Miocene), revised from an earlier estimate of about 12-13 million years.
The skull is about 3 m (10 ft) long.
The largest teeth exceed 36 cm (14 in), among the largest biting teeth of any known animal, excluding tusks.
Body length is estimated at 13.5-17.5 m (44-57 ft).
The genus was first named Leviathan but renamed Livyatan because Leviathan was already used for a mastodon.
The species name honours Herman Melville, author of Moby-Dick.
Unlike the modern sperm whale, Livyatan had large functional teeth in both upper and lower jaws.
Its skull has a large supracranial basin, suggesting a spermaceti organ.
Likely prey were medium-sized baleen whales of roughly 7-10 m (23-33 ft).
Megalodon teeth occur in the same Pisco Formation deposits and era.
Raptorial sperm whale teeth possibly attributable to Livyatan are known from Chile, South Africa and Australia.
Late Miocene cooling and changes in baleen whale prey may have contributed to its extinction (hypothesis).
The aquatic sloth Thalassocnus is known from the Pisco Formation.
